common_name: Hetz Midget Arborvitae (Extremely Compact Dwarf Globe Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Hetz Midget is among the smallest and slowest-growing arborvitae cultivars available, often taking decades to reach even modest size.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Hetz Midget forms an extremely dense, tidy, naturally globe-shaped mound of fine, bright green, scale-like foliage, growing so slowly that it needs virtually no pruning or shearing to maintain its neat form over many years, making it a low-maintenance choice for rock gardens, foundation plantings, and small-space landscapes where a full-size arborvitae would quickly overwhelm. Its diminutive scale and dense texture also suit it well to mixed conifer collections and formal edging. Like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates with consistent moisture and struggles in the extreme heat and humidity of the Deep South, so afternoon shade is helpful in warmer parts of its range. Established plants need only occasional deep watering during drought and essentially no shaping.

common_name: DeGroot's Spire Arborvitae (Narrow Columnar Twisted-Foliage Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; DeGroot's Spire holds an unusually narrow, tightly columnar form with distinctively twisted foliage sprays, fitting tight spaces where wider arborvitae cultivars would not.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, spacing plants closely if used as a narrow screen or accent row. DeGroot's Spire grows into a tight, formal, exclamation-point column of dark green foliage arranged in distinctive twisted, spiraling sprays that give the plant a subtly sculptural texture even without pruning, reaching a substantial height while staying remarkably narrow. Its slim profile makes it useful for tight side-yard screening, framing an entryway, or repeating as a vertical accent in a formal planting where wider columnar conifers would not fit. Like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates with consistent moisture and can struggle in extreme heat and humidity, so afternoon shade helps in the warmest parts of its range. Established plants need little pruning to maintain their naturally narrow form.

common_name: Danica Arborvitae (Very Dwarf Bright Green Globe Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Danica is a very dwarf, tightly globe-shaped Danish-bred arborvitae that stays compact for many years without pruning.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Danica forms a very dwarf, perfectly rounded globe of dense, bright green, fine-textured foliage that turns a warm bronze-green in winter cold before greening back up in spring, staying naturally compact for many years without any pruning or shearing. Its small, tidy scale makes it especially useful for rock gardens, low borders, container plantings, and small foundation beds where even the smallest standard arborvitae would eventually outgrow the space. Like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates with consistent moisture and can struggle in extreme summer heat and humidity, so afternoon shade helps where summers are hottest. Established plants need only occasional deep watering during drought and essentially no maintenance to keep their naturally neat form.

common_name: Golden Globe Arborvitae (Dwarf Rounded Golden-Yellow Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Golden Globe holds bright golden-yellow foliage color best with full sun exposure, fading toward chartreuse-green in shadier sites.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest, most consistent golden-yellow foliage color. Golden Globe forms a naturally dwarf, rounded mound of dense, bright gold foliage that holds its warm color through the growing season better than many other golden conifers, deepening slightly with a coppery cast in winter cold. Its compact, tidy habit needs little to no pruning to maintain shape, and its bright color makes it a strong focal accent among green-foliaged shrubs and conifers in a mixed border or foundation planting. Like other arborvitae it prefers cooler climates with consistent moisture and can struggle in extreme summer heat and humidity, so afternoon shade helps in the hottest parts of its range, though this will soften the gold color somewhat. Established plants need only occasional deep watering during drought.

common_name: Skyrocket Juniper (Extremely Narrow Columnar Blue-Gray Juniper)

planting.note: Plant in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic soil in full sun; Skyrocket forms one of the narrowest columnar conifers available, only 2-3 feet wide despite reaching 15-20 feet tall.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral or slightly acidic, dry to average soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential, as juniper roots rot quickly in consistently wet soil. Skyrocket forms an exceptionally narrow, tightly fastigiate column of soft blue-gray foliage, staying only 2-3 feet wide while eventually reaching 15-20 feet tall, making it one of the most useful conifers for tight side yards, narrow vertical accents, or repeating in a formal row where wider columnar evergreens would not fit. It is extremely drought-tolerant and cold-hardy once established, thriving in the lean, dry, rocky soils of its native Rocky Mountain and Great Plains range, and needs minimal pruning to maintain its naturally narrow form. Avoid overhead irrigation and overly rich, moisture-retentive soil, both of which increase susceptibility to twig blight and other fungal problems in humid climates.
